blocks.html:
This journey introduces no new method. It follows one binary-outcome question from design to a reported odds ratio, using §13.2.

Research question. In a CBHI household survey, is distance to the nearest health facility associated with CBHI membership, independent of household wealth and maternal education?

Study design. Cross-sectional survey of 500 households in 20 villages (25 per village), recording membership, distance (km), a wealth index and maternal education.

Outcome. CBHI membership, coded 1 = member, 0 = non-member. 150 of 500 households (30%) are members.

Exposure and confounders. Distance (continuous, km) is the exposure. Wealth (continuous index) and maternal education (none / primary / secondary-or-higher; reference: none) are confounders, chosen before fitting because each plausibly affects both where a household lives relative to a facility and whether it enrols (recall §11.6).

Why this method? A binary outcome, a mix of continuous and categorical predictors, and a question about an adjusted association: binary logistic regression (§13.2.3).

Data preparation. Education becomes two dummy variables against “none” (recall §12.4.3). Three households are recorded at 0 km; on review this is the code for “facility in the village”, so they are kept.

Crude analysis. Membership on distance alone: OR 0.85 per km (95% CI 0.80 to 0.90) (§13.2.3).

Model specification. Membership on distance, wealth and education together. 150 events for 4 coefficients gives an EPV of 37.5 (recall §13.2.4).

Assumptions. Linearity in the logit: adding quadratic terms for distance and wealth does not improve the fit (likelihood-ratio test, which compares the log-likelihoods of the two models, §15.1.4: p = 0.84). Separation: members and non-members occur across the whole range of distance and wealth and at every education level. Independence: households are clustered in villages. The ordinary model ignores this, so its SEs are likely too small; §15.2 refits the model with the clustering taken into account.

Diagnostics. Wealth and education are moderately correlated (Spearman ρ = 0.39), but every VIF is below 1.2 (recall §12.4.4.1), so each coefficient can be read on its own. Discrimination: the mean predicted probability is 0.39 among members and 0.26 among non-members, and the c-statistic is 0.72 (the probability that a randomly chosen member gets a higher predicted probability than a randomly chosen non-member; §15.5.2 develops it).

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
cb <- read.csv("data/cbhi_survey.csv")
cb$maternal_education <- factor(cb$maternal_education,
  levels = c("none", "primary", "secondary+"))
m1 <- glm(cbhi_member ~ distance_km + wealth_index +
            maternal_education,
          family = binomial, data = cb)
round(exp(cbind(OR = coef(m1), confint.default(m1))), 2)
nd <- data.frame(distance_km = 5, wealth_index = 0,
  maternal_education = factor("secondary+",
                              levels(cb$maternal_education)))
predict(m1, nd, type = "response")
                               OR 2.5 % 97.5 %
(Intercept)                  0.62  0.32   1.19
distance_km                  0.91  0.85   0.97
wealth_index                 1.34  1.18   1.53
maternal_educationprimary    1.29  0.76   2.20
maternal_educationsecondary+ 1.87  1.07   3.25
        1 
0.4194204

Each row after the intercept is an adjusted OR with its Wald 95% CI; these are the numbers in the Output table. The intercept, 0.62, is the odds of membership at 0 km, wealth index 0 and no maternal education (b₀ = −0.480). The last line is a predicted probability, worked by hand below.

blocks.label: Output.
blocks.html:
Predictor OR 95% CI p-value
Distance (per km) 0.91 0.85 to 0.97 0.005
Wealth index (per unit) 1.34 1.18 to 1.53 <0.001
Education: Primary 1.29 0.76 to 2.20 0.35
Education: Secondary+ 1.87 1.07 to 3.25 0.027

Worked Calculation (predicted probability)

A household 5 km from the facility, wealth index 0, mother with secondary education:

  1. Coefficients: b₀ = −0.480; distance −0.094 per km; secondary+ 0.625.
  2. Logit = −0.480 + 5 × (−0.094) + 0.625 = −0.325.
  3. p = 1 ÷ (1 + e^(0.325)) = 0.42.

Interpretation. Adjusting for wealth and education, each additional kilometre is associated with 9% lower odds of membership (OR 0.91, 95% CI 0.85 to 0.97); 5 km more multiplies the odds by 0.91⁵ = 0.62. The adjusted OR (0.91) is closer to 1 than the crude OR (0.85). Noncollapsibility alone would tend to move it the other way (recall §13.2.5), so the shift suggests that wealth and education confounded part of the crude association. Households whose mothers have secondary or higher education have 1.87 times the odds of membership of households with no maternal education (95% CI 1.07 to 3.25). The primary-education comparison is imprecise, and its CI includes 1.

What the result does not mean. Membership is common (30%), so these ORs are not risk ratios (recall §13.2.6). The same model fitted as a prevalence-ratio model (§13.7) gives 0.95 per km instead of 0.91, and 1.52 instead of 1.87 for secondary education. Nor does a cross-sectional association show that better roads would raise membership by a predictable amount: distance may stand for unmeasured remoteness (market access, outreach visits).

Reporting. “In a multivariable logistic regression adjusting for household wealth and maternal education, greater distance to the nearest health facility was associated with lower odds of CBHI membership (adjusted OR 0.91 per km, 95% CI 0.85–0.97, p = 0.005). Secondary or higher maternal education was associated with higher odds of membership than no education (adjusted OR 1.87, 95% CI 1.07–3.25, p = 0.027). Membership was common (30%), so the odds ratios overstate the corresponding prevalence ratios, and the cross-sectional design does not allow causal interpretation.”

points.html: Report the crude-to-adjusted change (0.85 → 0.91), but do not use it to choose confounders. Wealth and education were adjusted for because subject-matter reasoning marked them as confounders before the model was fitted; distance is the exposure.
Outcome coding and reference categories go into the reporting sentence.
State what the result does not mean in the same paragraph as the result.
